Would you be kind enough to direct me to any of these genetic test? I'd like to see what's being found and how the conclusions are drawn. Thanks!

Here's one published in an issue of the ICPS newsletter last year:
www.carnivorousplants.org/cpn/articles/CPNv44n2p82_84.pdf


This article suggests S. oreophila and S. purpurea are the most ancient species, so it still seems possible that the species could have all come from purpurea. The question is whether or not that's the full piece of the puzzle and is it that simple? If you think about all the populations that existed before humans destroyed everything, and then compound that diversity and go back maybe 100's of 1000's (if not millions) of years ago, probability would suggest the ancestors of various Sarracenia species today could have gone extinct in the way distant past. Let's also remember that the climate was different way back in time, so some Sarracenia ancestors may have evolved on different continents and then went extinct for all we know....

It's also very hard to interpret such linear data as found in many of these scientific studies. Historic hybridization many generations ago really creates a grey area when doing DNA comparisons.

posts.body_html:
There is this bit though:
"Contrary to previous genetic attempts at resolving the relationships within the genus, the purpurea complex is not basal to all other Sarracenia. Rather, this complex shares a recent common ancestor with psittacina/flava/minor."

I'm not trying to make any arguments from authority, this is just the only scientific data I've run across on the topic. I welcome any additional data or alternate theories, I don't have much of an opinion myself.

Mar 27, 2017 18:17:21 GMT -5 meizzwang said:
The beauty of linear data: 2 different people can interpret 2 completely opposite results using the same exact information.
Yes, indeed! Thank you alabamensis and Mike for the views and link. That was a good read. I took great interest in Taxonomy as a college student; worked in the Univ. herbarium and the U.S. National Arboretum herbarium as well. This gave ample time to ask a lot of brilliant people about plant names and naming philosophies. Of course, I prodded them with Sarracenia-scenario questions and the future prospect of gene analysis. Well... that begs the unanswered questions:
While quantitative similarities may indicate relationships, they do not answer which genes are most important in separating species. One gene/allele can result in a new species if that new species can not breed with others not sharing that gene. The mixing bowl which is Sarracenia reminds me of orchid taxonomy; many theories and philosophies. One could argue all Sarracenia are one species, since they are a (comparatively) recent genus and they interbreed easily, with the morphological difficulties of flava x psittacina aside. (Odd these show"close" relationship genetically when these are amongst the least likely to hybridize!)

Compare the Sarr. to, say, squash (Cucurbita) or Peppers (Capsicum): Cucurbita maxima, winter squash, does not hybridize with Cucurbita pepo, Acorn, Crookneck, Zucchini, etc. Likewise, Habanero peppers, Capsicum chinense, don't hybridize with Sweet peppers or Jalapeños, Capsicum annuum. Yet, all the Sarr. species are capable of interbreeding and frequently hybridize.

So, does anyone REALLY know what's going on? Chances are, there will be different philosophies for many years to come. Nature pushes genetics. Dynamic, changing habitats tend to encourage mutations necessary to survive. What one "sees" in quantitative genetic studies may ultimately reflect evolutionary pressures. This may or may not help decide how to name plants. In the end, we're working with a human-made construct.

posts.body_html:
bogman I am pretty sure nobody knows what's really going on, haha. A more knowledgeable person than myself on here once opined that modern taxonomy really isn't well suited to plants in general, and Sarracenia in particular. There is just too much gray and blurring of lines for a black-and-white system to work well. And the equally frustrating alternative is to see every subtle color variant accorded taxonomic status (not naming any names...). The good news is introgression has made the species so much more interesting from a horticultural perspective. We need a TSF shirt that says "I (heart) introgression" - I would rock that. 

This thread has some more on this topic if anyone wants to continue down the nerdy rabbit hole...
